submission:
Root cause: At 10:53:18, about six minutes before the 10:59:24 alert, platform-automation created a NetworkPolicy `deny-all-recommendation` recorded as namespace-wide rather than narrowly selected [tr_87652bf6467a][tr_0c99cf700f8c]. That policy cuts L3/L4 connectivity on the recommendation path inside the namespace, so frontend's calls on that edge no longer reach a peer. The mechanism is connectivity removal, not an application regression: frontend's change history holds no image bump, no flag toggle and no dependency change, only first-time creation of its Service and workload [tr_87652bf6467a], and its log shows a clean cold start at 10:53:05-10:53:06 that resolved all backends and reached a serving state, with no panic, exception, timeout or downstream error afterwards [tr_d3e4bb54f84b]. The Consul connection-refused lines at 10:53:05 precede the policy and clear within two seconds, so they are startup race noise. Frontend alerted because it is the caller that notices; what broke is the recommendation path being severed.
Faulty component: recommendation
Fault type: network_partition
Confidence: medium

Evidence:
- Three changes landed on frontend, all from the platform-automation actor within the same ~15-second span roughly 6 minutes before onset (10:53:03–10:53:18), making them tightly correlated with the incident timing. (found, from change_history on frontend)
- The highest-suspicion change is the creation of a namespace-wide deny-all NetworkPolicy, which the change record notes selects pods — a change class that can sever frontend ingress/egress connectivity without any application change. (found, from change_history on frontend)
- The other two changes are the initial creation of the frontend Service and the first creation of the workload container, indicating the frontend was being stood up fresh rather than modified in place. (found, from change_history on frontend)
- A code deploy or container image version bump to an existing frontend introduced a regression. (ruled_out, from change_history on frontend; why: No deploy or image-version-bump entries appear in the window; the only container event is a first-ever creation of the workload, not a replacement of a prior revision.)
- A feature flag was toggled shortly before the incident. (ruled_out, from change_history on frontend; why: The change history lists only config-created and container-created events; no flag toggle is recorded in the 24-hour window.)
- A dependency or library version bump on frontend caused the failure. (ruled_out, from change_history on frontend; why: No dependency version change is recorded among the three changes in the window.)
- Slow configuration drift or an older change hours earlier is responsible. (ruled_out, from change_history on frontend; why: The window spans a full 24 hours and contains only three changes, all clustered 6 minutes before onset; nothing landed earlier in the period.)
- A human operator made a manual change that triggered the incident. (ruled_out, from change_history on frontend; why: All three changes are attributed to the platform-automation actor, not a human.)
- A previously healthy, long-running frontend degraded on its own. (ruled_out, from change_history on frontend; why: The workload and Service were created for the first time 6 minutes before onset, so there was no prior steady-state instance to degrade.)
- All three recorded changes to profile in the window were landed by the same actor, platform-automation, clustered at 10:53:04-10:53:18, roughly six minutes before onset. (found, from change_history on profile)
- A deny-all NetworkPolicy affecting the recommendation path was created at 10:53:18 and is recorded as namespace-wide in scope rather than targeted at a narrow pod subset. (found, from change_history on profile)
- The profile Service and its backing workload were both created (not modified) at 10:53:04, fourteen seconds before the policy landed. (found, from change_history on profile)
- The change record carries an additional qualifier about the pods the policy selects, which reads as incomplete or malformed metadata; the selector's practical effect on profile pods is not fully established by this record alone. (found, from change_history on profile)
- The NetworkPolicy and the Service/workload changes came from different actors or pipelines, implying an uncoordinated collision between two teams. (ruled_out, from change_history on profile; why: All three changes are attributed to the single actor platform-automation within a fourteen-second span, so this is one automation rollout, not two colliding ones.)
- The deny-all policy is narrowly scoped to a specific pod selector and therefore would not affect the broader profile namespace. (ruled_out, from change_history on profile; why: The change record explicitly describes the policy scope as namespace-wide, so a narrow-blast-radius reading is not supported.)
- A regression was introduced by editing an existing, previously healthy Service or deployment for profile. (ruled_out, from change_history on profile; why: Both the Service and the workload are recorded as first creations in this window, so there is no prior working version that was mutated; this is initial stand-up, not a regression.)
- The relevant change landed well outside the 10:53 window and the timing correlation with onset is coincidental. (ruled_out, from change_history on profile; why: The change history for profile across a 24-hour window contains only these three entries, all six minutes before onset, leaving no competing change at another time.)
- The policy was in place before the workload came up, so pods were never reachable at any point. (ruled_out, from change_history on profile; why: Ordering shows the Service and workload created at 10:53:04 and the policy at 10:53:18, so there was a brief interval before the policy landed.)
- The frontend log stream for the 30-minute window contains no error or warning lines at or near 10:59:24; the only non-INFO lines in the entire window are clustered at 10:53:05, roughly six minutes before the time of interest. (found, from logql_query on frontend; query: {namespace="hotel-reservation",pod=~"frontend-([a-z0-9]+-[a-z0-9]+|[0-9]+)"})
- The error lines present at 10:53:05 are service-discovery failures: the frontend's Consul-backed gRPC load balancer could not retrieve instances for two named services (srv-profile and srv-search), failing with a TCP connection-refused to the Consul agent endpoint on port 8500. These repeat several times. (found, from logql_query on frontend; query: {namespace="hotel-reservation",pod=~"frontend-([a-z0-9]+-[a-z0-9]+|[0-9]+)"})
- The error type named is a connection refusal at dial time, not a timeout/deadline and not a language-level exception or panic. The named counterparty is the Consul agent (the discovery dependency), with srv-profile and srv-search appearing only as lookup targets, not as callees that returned errors. (found, from logql_query on frontend; query: {namespace="hotel-reservation",pod=~"frontend-([a-z0-9]+-[a-z0-9]+|[0-9]+)"})
- The surrounding INFO lines show a full cold-start sequence at 10:53:05-10:53:06 (config read, Jaeger init, Consul agent init, gRPC client initialization for search, profile, recommendation, reservation, user, then HTTP serving), indicating the frontend process restarted at 10:53:05 and reached a serving state by 10:53:06. (found, from logql_query on frontend; query: {namespace="hotel-reservation",pod=~"frontend-([a-z0-9]+-[a-z0-9]+|[0-9]+)"})
- The Consul discovery errors were transient relative to startup: they precede the successful gRPC client initialization lines and the serving confirmation in the same two-second span, and do not recur afterwards in the window. (found, from logql_query on frontend; query: {namespace="hotel-reservation",pod=~"frontend-([a-z0-9]+-[a-z0-9]+|[0-9]+)"})
- Frontend logged a downstream call failure (e.g. to search, profile, reservation, user, or recommendation) at 10:59:24 that identifies the faulty service (ruled_out, from logql_query on frontend; why: No log lines of any level exist at or around 10:59:24 in this window; the stream's last entry is at 10:53:06. Frontend logs cannot supply a callee name for that moment.; query: {namespace="hotel-reservation",pod=~"frontend-([a-z0-9]+-[a-z0-9]+|[0-9]+)"})
- Frontend was hitting gRPC deadline-exceeded / request timeouts on a downstream dependency (ruled_out, from logql_query on frontend; why: The only failures captured are dial-time connection-refused errors against Consul. No timeout, deadline, or context-cancellation wording appears anywhere in the window.; query: {namespace="hotel-reservation",pod=~"frontend-([a-z0-9]+-[a-z0-9]+|[0-9]+)"})
- Frontend crashed or was failing due to an unhandled exception/panic in application code (ruled_out, from logql_query on frontend; why: No exception type, panic, or stack trace appears. The restart at 10:53:05 is followed by a clean init sequence and a successful serve, consistent with a normal process start rather than a code fault.; query: {namespace="hotel-reservation",pod=~"frontend-([a-z0-9]+-[a-z0-9]+|[0-9]+)"})
- Frontend ran continuously throughout the window and the incident is purely downstream (ruled_out, from logql_query on frontend; why: A complete cold-start sequence appears at 10:53:05, showing the frontend pod restarted mid-window. A frontend-side restart event must be accounted for in the timeline.; query: {namespace="hotel-reservation",pod=~"frontend-([a-z0-9]+-[a-z0-9]+|[0-9]+)"})
- Consul was permanently unreachable and the frontend never came up / never resolved its backends (ruled_out, from logql_query on frontend; why: After the connection-refused bursts, the frontend logs successful gRPC connection setup for all five backends and reports serving HTTP within one second, so discovery recovered.; query: {namespace="hotel-reservation",pod=~"frontend-([a-z0-9]+-[a-z0-9]+|[0-9]+)"})
- Only one backend dependency was affected at startup (ruled_out, from logql_query on frontend; why: The discovery failures name two distinct services and share a single cause (the Consul endpoint refusing connections), indicating a dependency-wide condition rather than one bad backend.; query: {namespace="hotel-reservation",pod=~"frontend-([a-z0-9]+-[a-z0-9]+|[0-9]+)"})
- A trace query for the frontend service across the full 30-minute window ending 10:59:29 returned no spans at all — not merely at the 10:59:24 mark, but for the entire interval. (found, from trace_query on frontend)
- Because no frontend spans exist, there is no trace-side record of outbound calls to profile, search, reservation, user, or recommendation — neither successful, nor erroring, nor connection-refused. The question of 'failing vs. ceasing' cannot be answered from traces; the spans are simply absent. (found, from trace_query on frontend)
- The absence is uniform rather than onset-shaped, which is more consistent with frontend emitting/exporting no telemetry for the whole window (or the traces not reaching the backend) than with a service that was healthy and then degraded at 10:59:24. (found, from trace_query on frontend)
- Frontend was still handling requests and its traces would show connection-level errors (refused/reset/timeout) on calls to the downstream services, pinpointing which dependency broke first. (ruled_out, from trace_query on frontend; why: No frontend spans exist in the window, so no error-tagged client spans toward any downstream service can be observed. This line of evidence is unavailable and cannot support a per-dependency blame assignment.)
- A specific downstream dependency (e.g. profile or reservation) can be identified as the trigger by comparing when each outbound span type stopped. (ruled_out, from trace_query on frontend; why: All outbound span types are equally absent for the entire window, giving no differential timing between dependencies to compare.)
- The disruption was a brief blip localized to ~10:59:24. (ruled_out, from trace_query on frontend; why: The trace gap covers the full 30 minutes from 10:29:24, so whatever the trace backend reflects is not a momentary event at the window's end.)
- Traces will serve as the primary timeline for frontend behavior during this incident. (ruled_out, from trace_query on frontend; why: The trace source is empty for this service and window; the timeline must be reconstructed from logs, metrics, or deploy/config events instead.)
- The error-ratio metric query for frontend over the incident window returned no data at all; the backend reports that it holds no span-derived metrics for this service because frontend does not emit traces that are converted into metrics. (found, from metric_baseline on frontend)
- Consequently no error rate, request rate, or latency percentile values for frontend at or around 10:59:24 can be established from this source, and the four outbound edges (productcatalog, cart, ad, recommendation) cannot be compared for error or latency shifts at that minute via span metrics. (found, from metric_baseline on frontend)
- The comparison baseline window (09:59:19-10:29:24) is equally unpopulated, so there is no before/after contrast available from this instrument. (found, from metric_baseline on frontend)
- frontend's span metrics show a clean, error-free period, so the fault lies downstream. (ruled_out, from metric_baseline on frontend; why: The result is an explicit query failure, not a zero-valued series. Absence of data here carries no information about frontend health and cannot be read as evidence of no errors.)
- A spike in frontend error ratio or latency percentiles at 10:59:24 can be confirmed or timed from Prometheus span metrics. (ruled_out, from metric_baseline on frontend; why: The metric family required for that confirmation does not exist in this Prometheus for frontend, so neither confirmation nor refutation is obtainable from this path.)
- The empty result reflects a transient scrape gap or a window chosen outside data retention. (ruled_out, from metric_baseline on frontend; why: The backend gives a structural reason - frontend emits no traces that become metrics - which applies to both the incident and baseline windows rather than to a specific time range.)
- Per-edge error or latency attribution across frontend's four outbound dependencies can be derived from this metric source. (ruled_out, from metric_baseline on frontend; why: Edge-level breakdowns are themselves span-derived; with no span metrics for frontend, no edge series exist to inspect.)

Reasoning:
Change history across a full 24 hours for two services contains exactly one suspicious act: the namespace-wide deny-all NetworkPolicy at 10:53:18, everything else being first-time stand-up of Services and workloads [tr_87652bf6467a][tr_0c99cf700f8c]. Frontend's log rules out the application-side stories - no deadline or context-cancellation wording, no panic or stack trace, and successful gRPC client init followed by an HTTP serving confirmation [tr_d3e4bb54f84b]; a crash or a slow dependency would have left one of those. The silent instruments are not negative evidence: the Prometheus error-ratio queries for frontend and profile failed structurally because neither emits span-derived metrics, over both incident and baseline windows [tr_2cca751ac3a4][tr_5dc2642b7db7], and the Tempo gap for frontend is uniform across the whole 30 minutes rather than onset-shaped [tr_2905d9ddfa34]. A deny-all policy named for the recommendation path is the mechanism that hangs a caller on one edge while the callee's process stays up - partition, not a wrong configuration value breaking a request. The fix is restoring the severed connectivity.

Alternatives considered:
1. frontend: The same namespace-wide deny-all policy isolates frontend itself rather than recommendation, cutting it off from all five backends. (network_partition). Ranked lower because: Same policy and mechanism, different victim, and the evidence barely separates them. It ranks second only because the policy is named for the recommendation path; frontend's log ends twelve seconds before the policy landed, so there is no post-policy frontend signal either way. One dispatch to recommendation could invert this.
2. frontend: The policy's scope value is itself wrong - written namespace-wide when a narrow selector was intended - making the misconfiguration the failure. (bad_config). Ranked lower because: The wrong value is how this started, but what is happening now is severed connectivity; classifying by the upstream edit rather than the live mechanism. Reverting the policy is still the practical fix, so the two converge in action if not in class.

Open questions:
- No dispatch reached recommendation itself; its logs would decide partition versus freeze, since a partitioned process complains it cannot reach anything and a frozen one writes nothing.
- The policy's real selector is unresolved - one finding calls the selector metadata incomplete and says its practical effect is not established [tr_0c99cf700f8c], so the blast radius and the named service could both change.
- Frontend wrote nothing after 10:53:06 [tr_d3e4bb54f84b] and emitted no spans all window [tr_2905d9ddfa34], so whether it was serving traffic at 10:59:24 - and why onset lagged the policy by six minutes - is unverified.
